answers.answer: The stub is the client's local lookup helper and asks the recursive resolver to obtain the answer. A zone is a managed portion of DNS names; its authoritative servers supply its records. Delegation assigns a child zone to its authorities, and a referral points toward them rather than supplying the final host address. With empty relevant caches the recursive resolver asks root, follows its .example referral, follows .example's notes.example referral, and obtains authoritative records for api.notes.example. Its CNAME aliases edge.notes.example; usable target A (IPv4) or AAAA (IPv6) address data is required, whether returned with the alias or obtained through another lookup. The resolver returns the result to the stub and the client uses an address family it can reach. Later cached answers can avoid authority visits, cached delegations can shorten the route, and alias and target data can be cached separately. DNS resolves api.notes.example, not /notes/42. The client connects to a usable address, verifies HTTPS for api.notes.example, and sends the HTTP request including /notes/42 over that encrypted connection. An address answer does not establish Notes health.

evidence.quote: The stub resolver is the client's local lookup helper. It asks a recursive resolver to obtain an answer on its behalf. An authoritative server supplies records for a zone, a managed portion of DNS names.
Delegation assigns responsibility for a child zone to its authoritative servers. A referral points the resolver toward them; it is not the final host address.
A CNAME record is a name alias. Resolving it follows the target name to obtain A or AAAA data, possibly already cached or returned with the alias. Otherwise another lookup is needed.
IPv4 and IPv6 are two IP address families. An A record supplies an IPv4 address; an AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address. A client uses an address family it can reach.
DNS resolves the hostname, not the URL path, and does not carry the later HTTP exchange.
An address answer does not establish that the application is healthy.

answers.answer: TTL limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds, with each cache aging the TTL it received. The old answer cached at 11:59 with 3600 seconds can remain ordinarily usable until 12:59, so it need not refresh by 12:01; the noon 60-second edit cannot rewrite its entry. For a safer move, lower TTL first and wait for the previous 3600-second lifetime to age out before switching. Keep the old destination usable throughout the transition, monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. The lesson supplies no fixed universal shutdown time: independent caches, existing connections and possible expired-data serving during failed refreshes require observing clients, not assuming all traffic has moved at one deadline. Shorter TTLs increase refresh queries and dependence on working DNS. TTL is not a global update timer and DNS changes do not move open connections.

evidence.quote: TTL, or time to live, limits ordinary cache reuse in seconds. Each cache ages the TTL it received; it is not a worldwide update timer.

For a planned move, lower TTL first, allow the previous longer TTL to age out, then switch. Keep the old destination usable through the transition while monitoring traffic, errors and existing connections at both destinations. DNS edits do not migrate open connections.

Shorter TTLs mean more refresh queries and more frequent dependence on working DNS. Independent caches and connection lifetimes prevent a simultaneous cutover. Some resolvers can even serve expired data when refreshing fails, so TTL is not a hard global recovery deadline.

answers.answer: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. The cached NXDOMAIN says api.notes.example did not exist; adding an A record does not notify that cache. Its own negative cache lifetime governs reuse, so the new positive record's 30-second TTL does not clear it and the lesson gives no exact remaining negative lifetime here. NXDOMAIN reports name absence. NODATA for AAAA reports an existing name without that requested type; it does not establish absence of an A record or of the name. SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, not that the name does not exist. Failures may also be cached to avoid hammering failing DNS servers. Inspect requested name, type and status to distinguish these cases before changing records.

evidence.quote: Negative caching reuses an answer reporting absence. NXDOMAIN says the queried name does not exist. NODATA means the name exists but has no record of the requested type: no AAAA record does not imply no A record or no name.
The negative answer has its own cache lifetime; the new positive record's TTL does not clear it.

SERVFAIL means resolution could not be completed, for example because the resolver could not obtain usable answers. It is not proof that the name does not exist. Resolution failures may also be cached to avoid repeatedly hammering failing DNS servers.

answers.answer: DNS steering selects destinations returned in answers; failover changes that selection after failure. A separate health check and policy or an operator must detect east's failure and change answers, since ordinary records do not detect application health. Equal lookup answers do not imply equal HTTP traffic: a shared recursive resolver reuses an answer for many clients and each client can send many requests on that address or connection. Removing east from new answers leaves cached clients still able to try east and cannot migrate existing connections to west. West must be reachable, healthy and have spare capacity for redirected work. A health signal is only a sample; changing DNS neither creates capacity nor guarantees instant recovery.

evidence.quote: DNS traffic steering selects destinations returned in answers. Failover changes the selected destination after failure.
For east and west endpoints, a separate health check and policy, or an operator, must detect east's failure and change answers. Ordinary DNS records do not detect application health themselves.
A shared recursive resolver can reuse one answer for many clients, and each client may send many requests using that address or connection.
After east is removed from new answers, cached clients can still try it. Existing connections do not migrate to west just because DNS changed.
West must be reachable, healthy and have enough spare capacity for redirected work.

answers.answer: Users with usable cached addresses may still connect during a DNS outage, and existing open connections may keep working without lookup. New uncached clients need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and answering authoritative servers. Begin at the client's recursive resolver: inspect the exact name, record type, answer/error and remaining TTL; compare authoritative data and parent delegation for wrong or failing results. An authoritative new address alongside a cached old one suggests cache aging rather than another immediate edit. If the expected address resolves, investigate connection, HTTPS and application results separately. HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error, not by itself DNS lookup failure; successful DNS does not prove Notes works. Reachable alternate resolvers and authorities reduce individual DNS server failures, but cannot fix shared wrong records, broken delegation or a failed application. Multiple servers with identical bad configuration can return the same wrong result.

evidence.quote: During a DNS outage, a client with a usable cached address may still connect, and an open connection may keep working without a lookup. Fresh uncached lookups need a reachable recursive resolver, working delegation and authoritative servers that can answer.

Start with the client's recursive resolver: inspect the queried name and type, its answer or error, and remaining TTL. Compare authoritative data and parent delegation when results are wrong or failing.
HTTP 500 means an HTTP service responded with an error; it is not by itself a DNS lookup failure.
Reachable alternate resolvers and authoritative servers reduce individual server failures. They cannot fix a shared wrong record, broken delegation or a failed application.

answers.answer: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks them through a chain of trust beginning at a configured trusted key, with each trusted signing key vouching for the next link. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity: alteration is detectable. It does not hide the query, certify Notes health or guarantee availability. Merely using a DNSSEC-supporting resolver does not add signature checks to unsigned data. HTTPS still separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange. The client must verify api.notes.example, its requested hostname, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.notes.example. DNSSEC validation does not remove those certificate checks or application access rules.

evidence.quote: DNSSEC adds signatures to DNS data. A validating resolver checks those signatures through a chain of trust: each trusted signing key vouches for the next link, starting at a configured trusted key. Successful validation establishes the signed data's origin and integrity, meaning it has not been altered without detection.
DNSSEC does not encrypt the query, certify service health or guarantee availability.
HTTPS separately authenticates the endpoint through certificate validation and encrypts the HTTP exchange.
The client must still verify the certificate for the hostname it requested, api.example.test, even if DNS followed an alias to edge.example.test.
